name: Antinatalism
scope: Philosophical antinatalism: the view that procreation is wrong or unjustifiable, in its local form (wrong in particular cases, as when a child would have a life not worth living) and above all its global form, that procreation as such is a harm or wrong, argued from Benatar's asymmetry, the harm of existence, lack of consent, misanthropic and environmental reasons (SEP 'Parenthood and Procreation' section 2.2; Coates, Singh). It follows the line the book-length scholarship traces from Schopenhauer, von Hartmann and Zapffe to Benatar's 2006 Better Never to Have Been, with Benatar the key figure (Singh). The voluntary-population-reduction strand of the activist movement (Church of Euthanasia, VHEMT, Korda) is included only as far as it states antinatalism itself. It excludes states' antinatalist population policies and the religious and literary rejectionism of existence that Coates treats as background (Hinduism, Buddhism, Beckett, Sartre) except where they speak to procreation.

keyFigures.quote: A little-known Norwegian philosopher and writer, Peter Wessel Zapffe (1899-1990), who may also be considered an existentialist, joins the company of Cioran in being a rejectionist and an anti-natalist.

keyFigures.role: Pessimist philosopher whose view of existence is anti-natal in its implications
keyFigures.quote: Arthur Schopenhauer (1851), for instance, is perhaps best known for advocating a pessimistic philosophy that is, broadly speaking, anti-natal in its implications.

keyFigures.role: 19th-century pessimist who looked to the gradual phasing out of human existence

summary: Antinatalism is the view that procreation is wrong or unjustifiable. Its global form, led by Benatar's asymmetry argument, holds that coming into existence is always a harm, so people should not have children; arguments from lack of consent, misanthropy and environmental harm are also made. Benatar rejects a state ban and asks for voluntary non-procreation and a planned, gradual end of the species, and the tradition runs back through Zapffe, von Hartmann and Schopenhauer.
